MR. DINSDALE-LETTER RESPECTING NATIONAL PARKS TABLED BY MINISTER OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. Yesterday afternoon the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development tabled a letter bearing my signature. I was out of the House attending a meeting with the chairman of the Canadian Transport Commission, the Hon. Jack Pickersgill, in the company of the Premier of Manitoba, the Manitoba Minister of Industry and Commerce and the mayor of Brandon.

subtopic: MR. DINSDALE-LETTER RESPECTING NATIONAL PARKS TABLED BY MINISTER OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: What a group!

subtopic: MR. DINSDALE-LETTER RESPECTING NATIONAL PARKS TABLED BY MINISTER OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
The meeting was convened to discuss ways and means for continuing the present class one air service into western Manitoba which has been threatened by Transair's application to suspend the service. Because of the implications of the proposed change in regional air policy for continuing economic progress in western Manitoba, I think you will agree that the meeting had top priority. This, then, is the first opportunity I have had to deal with the minister's action.
The issue raised in the House yesterday brings into focus the whole question of leaseholds in western national parks. It is also closely tied in to the feeling of isolation and alienation that is growing to an alarming degree in western and northwestern Canada, as has been pointed out recently in press articles. The government has demonstrated a congenital incapacity to deal with the serious special problems in these important areas of Canada.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. DINSDALE-LETTER RESPECTING NATIONAL PARKS TABLED BY MINISTER OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Order, please. I have to interrupt the hon. gentleman immediately to remind him that he has the floor now under very special rules and the requirement at this time is that he should indicate how his privileges as a member of this House have been violated by the tabling of the letter to which
he alludes in the notice he has given me. If he will indicate in what way he thinks there has been a breach of privilege, then further action might be contemplated. Certainly this is not the time to discuss the general policy which is perhaps the background of the tabling of the letter yesterday by the minister.

subtopic: MR. DINSDALE-LETTER RESPECTING NATIONAL PARKS TABLED BY MINISTER OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
I accept your ruling, Mr. Speaker. I merely made that reference because the problem is peculiar to the west inasmuch as there are no national parks in Quebec and only minor ones in Ontario. In tabling the letter the minister implied that it endorsed a policy that the Liberal government has been pursuing in respect of western national parks since 1963.
My question of privilege revolves around two fundamental matters: first, the right of the minister to table a letter signed by another Privy Councillor without first seeking the customary permission from the author and, second, the ethics of using this kind of cheap politics to stir up further trouble in the west.
The letter, of course, in no way endorses what the minister is attempting to do in the western parks today. It merely outlines the orderly plan that was adopted in 1962 for the development of national parks in western Canada based on the principles of wise management and multi-use that emerged out of the Resources for Tomorrow Conference in 1961. It carefully preserves the right of perpetuity in the original leases.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
Mr. Speaker, the letter was tabled. It is now the property of the House. It was tabled without my permission, and I do not think hon. members will have the opportunity of perusing it unless they make special efforts to do so.
The implication was left by the minister that it endorses his policy. I shall be as brief as I can on this fundamental point. It does not endorse that policy because the minister has arbitrarily cancelled perpetuity in original leases. The issue was taken to the Exchequer Court by the residents of the western parks and their position was upheld by that court. The minister has now referred the matter to

January 21, 1970
Privilege
the Supreme Court, hoping to get that decision reversed. It is because of these situations that there is a growing feeling of alienation.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the same situation is involved in the question asked by the hon. member for Oxford with reference to the rental reassessments that are now taking place in the national parks. This, again, was a policy agreed to only after long consultation with the advisory councils and the people in the parks, and it has nothing to do with the current increases of up to 4,000 per cent.
On the strength of the points I have made, Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that I be allowed to table some documents, with the consent of the House, which put the record straight. I am sure all hon. members would want this to be done in light of the distortions arising from the discussion yesterday.

subtopic: MR. DINSDALE-LETTER RESPECTING NATIONAL PARKS TABLED BY MINISTER OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. DINSDALE-LETTER RESPECTING NATIONAL PARKS TABLED BY MINISTER OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Order, please. As I indicated a moment ago, the hon. member got the floor on a question of privilege of which he had given the Chair due notice according to the Standing Orders. The observations of the hon. member were not followed by a motion so that in the ordinary way we cannot pursue the matter further. In any event, I have serious doubts whether there is an actual question of privilege.
The minister tabled the letter or document yesterday under the provisions of Standing Order 41(2) which gives a minister the right at any time to table a document or a paper. The hon. member suggested that the minister should perhaps have obtained his prior consent or permission. This is certainly not a requirement under the Standing Order and the Chair has to be guided by the Standing Orders.
I respectfully suggest to the hon. member that it would have been competent for any hon. member, under a motion for production of papers, to request the tabling of this and any other paper in the possession of the minister, under the terms of the Standing Orders. This is perhaps all obiter dicta because the hon. member has made his point. He has not followed his point by a formal motion which the Chair would have to put to the House. That would conclude my ruling on the question of privilege raised by the hon. member.
As a sequel to his observations he has suggested that additional papers might be tabled. The House is responsible for its own procedures. The House can accept the tabling of any documents whether it be by a minister or

by a private member on one side or other of the House. If that were the wish of the House I am sure that so far as the Chair is concerned there is no objection to the tabling of the documents to which the hon. member for Brandon-Souris has alluded. But that would not be in accordance with any of the Standing Orders of the House. Standing Order 41 to which I have referred, under which the minister has tabled the letter in question, provides as follows:
A Minister of the Crown, or a Parliamentary Secretary acting on behalf of a Minister, may, in his place in the House, state that he proposes to lay upon the Table of the House, any report or other paper dealing with a matter coming within the administrative responsibilities of the government-
That Standing Order does not appear to extend to a private member. If there is unanimous consent the papers can be received at the table. If there is not unanimous consent perhaps the hon. member would wish to seek another way of bringing them to the attention of the House. Is there unanimous consent?

subtopic: MR. DINSDALE-LETTER RESPECTING NATIONAL PARKS TABLED BY MINISTER OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Agreed.

subtopic: MR. DINSDALE-LETTER RESPECTING NATIONAL PARKS TABLED BY MINISTER OF INDIAN AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: We should not get into debate on this matter. I do not make the rules. I took the trouble of reading all of the Standing Order and it gives the minister the right to table the document. If there is agreement by all hon. members that additional documents be tabled the Chair, as I said, has no objection, but my ruling is simply a reading of the Standing Order. I did not write it. The Standing Order is a rule of the House, and I can only bring it to the attention of hon. members. It is unfortunate if the Standing Order has the effect that the hon. member suggests and difficulties result, but I would not think I am in a position to rectify the situation as a procedural matter.

That the abandonment by the government of the Canada Newstart Program be referred to the Standing Committee on Regional Development for consideration and report, and
That the Standing Committee on Regional Development be convened for purposes of organization.

STUDIES OF PHARMACEUTICAL FIRMS' DRUG TESTS
speechtext:
1.	Is the Food and Drug Directorate of the Department of National Health and Welfare undertaking special studies to evaluate whether drug tests submitted to the Directorate by pharmaceutical firms are ineptly designed and deficient, as disclosed in some tests reported in the United States.
2.	Is the government considering legislation which would take away the major responsibility for evaluating new drugs from the pharmaceutical manufacturers and give it to the federal government?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: STUDIES OF PHARMACEUTICAL FIRMS' DRUG TESTS
speechtext:
1. The Food and Drug Regulations require pharmaceutical manufacturers to submit details of all animal and clinical studies to the Food and Drug Directorate of the Department of National Health and Welfare before a new drug is marketed. This research data is carefully assessed and evaluated by officers in the Directorate. If the safety and effectiveness of the drug has not been clearly demonstrated, either by reason of deficient or poorly designed studies, the Notice of Compliance is withheld until properly designed studies have been conducted. In addition, officers of the Directorate frequently discuss proposed plans for both animal and clinical studies with manufacturers and with individual investigators.
2.	The majority of new drugs that reach the market are the result of the research and development activities of the pharmaceutical industry. Existing legislation under the Food and Drugs Act ensures that a proper evaluation of the safety and efficacy of all new drugs is made before they reach the Canadian market.

January 21. 1970
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)

The House resumed from Monday, January 19, consideration of the motion of Mr. Greene that Bill C-144, to provide for the management of the water resources of Canada including research and the planning and implementation of programs relating to the conservation development and utilization of water resources, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT INCLUDING RESEARCH AND PLANNING AND IMPLEMENTATION OF PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in taking part in this debate today, I should like to commence my remarks by stating how extremely gratifying it is to many of us as elected representatives to observe the very great interest Canadians are taking in the subject of pollution. More and more people are becoming deeply interested in the implementation of methods to control or eliminate, to the greatest possible extent, the pollution of our environment. Until about ten years ago, water pollution did not seem to attract much attention. When I first came to this House some years ago many statements were made by my colleagues and myself to the effect that water would probably become one of Canada's greatest natural resources, but at that time there was not the interest in the subject that there is today.
Mind you, some Canadians do not seem to realize that this House is debating the matter. I have contacted many of my constituents and some have stated how pleased they are to see the government taking some action, whilst others do not seem to know that the debate is taking place. However, even those who mentioned their interest in the government's action did not seem to have had an opportunity of perusing Bill C-144. If they had read it I am sure they would have realized, as we do, that this bill is an inadequate measure to control pollution. As I mentioned before, the Canadian people have been demanding an end to the continual corruption of the environment. We in the Progressive Conservative Party have continually recommended action against pollution and the government has responded with the Canada water act. This, I feel, is a pitifully weak bill, one which 
betrays the hopes and expectations of concerned Canadians. It simply does not provide any basis for effective action.
Members of our party are concerned and disturbed at the absence of comment in depth outside Parliament. Despite the profuse writings on the dangers of pollution, the dire warnings on the future of mankind and the constant call for action, there seems to have been very little study of the real content of the bill. The advance publicity last summer, and the flowery words of the minister as to his hopes and aspirations when introducing the bill, seem to have had the desired effect of lulling the country into a feeling of satisfaction. It is easy enough to understand the silence of industrial concerns and interests against whom the real control program would be directed, because they can see immediately the inadequacies of it and find no danger to themselves in it. The bill made its appearance well before Christmas and debate began on it almost immediately but many concerned Canadian writers have not had the opportunity to fully examine it.
We of the Progressive Conservative Party, the official opposition, are appealing for public support in our fight against a largely useless piece of legislation. We ask all those people concerned about pollution control to study this bill and to give opinions on it, because only an outraged public can force the government to strengthen its proposals and put teeth into this bill; and teeth are very, very necessary. I think that this points out very clearly one of the great values of Parliament. The government seems to play down the role of government and feels that it does not have a great role to play in our democratic society. However, I think this is one matter which is of great concern to all Canadians, and once again it demonstrates the value of Parliament and the value of debate.
As I said before, and I wish to underline this, I think it is very, very important for all Canadians interested in controlling and eliminating pollution as far as possible to read Bill C-144 and find out for themselves just what we of the opposition are trying to bring to the government's attention. We want to emphasize the idea that it is necessary to have amendments to this bill.
The success of the Canada water act is based on the fond hope that the federal government can persuade the provinces and municipalities to set up dozens of new water management boards without federal money, without national standards and without
January 21, 1970



proper research. Then, they will have to persuade the boards to collect their own money, organize their own projects and do battle with water pollution, with nothing from the federal government but advice and the inevitable necessity of having everything approved at provincial and federal levels. The result will be a new form of pollution, namely, large bundles of red tape.
Our party has clearly set out its alternative proposals on many occasions, dating back in their present form for two years. We would have the federal parliament pass a law applying to federal jurisdiction and proceed alone, where possible, or by agreement when working in a divided jurisdiction. Yet, we would go along with the government's plan if it had any real strength or hope of success. In its present form we see neither. It must be substantially re-written.
Recently we experienced a situation with respect to the Saskatchewan River in which serious contamination occurred as a result of mercury pollution. This has resulted in almost all of the species of fish in the lakes which are formed by this river downstream from the source of pollution being declared unfit for human consumption. I might add that this has taken place in a lucrative fishing area. I hope it will once again become lucrative for fishermen.
A considerable number of people residing downstream from the source of this contamination derive a good portion of their livelihood from commercial fishing, including a number of our Indian citizens, and their catches during the last month of yellows or pickerel, jacks and sauger have been ordered destroyed. The white fish on the other hand have been given a clean bill of health, apparently because they are not predator fish. I hasten to add at this time that the recently established freshwater fish marketing board has continued to purchase the contaminated fish from the commercial fishermen; but there will be an additional cost for destroying them.
In answer to questions in the House last week, the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis) said that the fisheries task force on the prairies had visited the plant of interprovincial co-operative downstream from Saskatoon and were of the opinion that this Chlor-Alkali plant is the principal if not the only source of mercury pollution on the prairies.
Answering a question of mine in the House yesterday, the Minister of Fisheries and
Water Resources
Forestry said, as reported on page 2583 of Hansard:
The necessary steps have been taken to make sure the effluent stream containing mercury is kept within the plant itselt. Mercury is meanwhile being removed by treating the effluent.
Naturally, we were very, very pleased to hear this statement and I am sure it will be well received by the fishermen concerned on the lakes downstream from the polluted area. But we are left with this further thought. For instance, it would be very interesting to know whether this was a voluntary move on the part of the industry concerned or whether the government had authority to order that this be done. I hope the minister will make a statement in the House and tell us just how this solution was arrived at in this particular instance.
Answering a supplementary question, the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry said that it will take a spring freshet to flush out the river completely. That also brings up interesting problems because the river, as the minister no doubt knows, empties into Lake Winnipeg. I am wondering, as are many other people, just what will happen to this mercury pollution when it is flushed out of the river and into Lake Winnipeg. Of course, it will go into the Nelson River and, eventually, into Hudson Bay. I can recall years ago, when asking questions in the House about the quality of water in northern Manitoba rivers such as the Nelson, being assured by the minister of the day that inspections were taking place from time to time and that there was no occasion for any of us to be concerned about the purity of the water in the Nelson river. Well, this is not the first time that we have seen pollution coming from the Saskatchewan River which empties into Lake Winnipeg. The water then flows from Lake Winnipeg out through the Nelson River.
Undoubtedly pollution is a very, very important subject for our consideration and I, personally, think it is one of the most important matters confronting Canada today. I could mention many other important subjects, such as inflation, national unity, unrest among our youth, the population explosion, poverty and aggression by force. All these are very, very pressing problems. However, I think that the question of pollution and pollution control ought to have a priority at least equal to that of many of the most important problems confronting us and should have greater priority than some.

January 21, 1970
Water Resources
I am quite sure that a reasonable person will realize that this bill dealing with pollution ought to be in the same category as any bill dealing with inflation, national unity, unrest among our youth and so on. But he could well expect to be charged with being an alarmist. Without doubt, at least one minister on the government's treasury benches feels that the people who talk this way are alarmists. I am sorry that the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry is not here today, because I should like to read to him some statements he has made on this very matter. Of course, in doing so I shall be trying to demonstrate that the government is not too concerned about the matter, as evidenced by the contents of Bill C-144.
Speaking to the Vancouver Chamber of Commerce last Thursday, the minister said that he does not subscribe to alarmist thought about pollution. I quote from what the minister said:
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
"I don't believe all that I read about dying lakes and sickening seas. Most of it is poppycock-written by novices who are reaching for headlines-"
I have already mentioned that I feel pollution deserves top priority, along with the other subjects I mentioned of inflation, national unity, unrest among our youth, population explosion and aggression by forces. The Minister of Fisheries and Forestry said people who talk like this are alarmists, that most of it is poppycock and they are novices reaching for headlines.
I have a document which was introduced in this House earlier this session. I quote from it as follows:
The evidence of past failure to rehabilitate our water resources is there for all to see-befouled water, despoiled beaches, rotting marine vegetation, and diminished fishing.
The document I am quoting from is the Speech from the Throne introduced in this House by the government.

speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT INCLUDING RESEARCH AND PLANNING AND IMPLEMENTATION OF PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Here we have the Minister of Fisheries saying that people who talk in an alarmist fashion are nothing but novices reaching for headlines. I think this is a clear example of one of the ministers of the treasury benches strongly disagreeing with those who support the tidying up mentioned in the Speech from the Throne.
The minister went further when he said, "the ecological situation is still basically under control". I do not know where the min-
ister finds any basis for saying this when all the reports, and the Speech from the Throne, admit that we have diminished fishing. That in itself upsets the ecological balance.
I have some interesting information before me, Mr. Speaker. It is contained in a letter written to Mr. R. C. Passmore, the Executive Director of the Canadian Wildlife Federation. This letter is signed by the President of the Flin Flon Wildlife Association. It is further evidence of the interest that wildlife and conservation groups are showing in this very important subject. The letter advises that a conservation seminar was sponsored by the Flin Flon Wildlife Association on January 10. The seminar was entitled "The Value of Water as a Natural Resource".
There were two papers presented, and I quote from a report:
The morning paper, "Water and Man" was given by Nes Mudry, Chief of the Planning Division, Water Control and Conservation Branch, Dept, of Mines and Natural Resources, Manitoba. The other paper was given by Jack Howard who is a biologist with the Manitoba Renewable Resources Branch.
The House may be interested in some of the findings:
At the morning session an attempt was made to define clean water and to identify some of the problems and pressures affecting our water resource. They decided that water was clean when it could be taken directly from a lake or stream and used for human consumption.
Over the years, this idea has been in the minds of the people living in our northern areas. Up until now they have had the advantage of an abundance of fresh water in lakes, water which could be taken directly out of the lakes and used for human consumption. These people are very concerned about the fact that pollution can and is taking place slowly but surely and will continue to increase unless strong measures are taken to control it.
I continue quoting:
Pollution was high on the fist of problems-not only industrial pollution but people pollution too. Further, all the groups agreed that Canada should not export water, that if industry needs water, then it should be required to move to the water and not vice versa.
-the participants were asked to make recommendations that would correct some of the problems. And here, I think, a rather amazing thing happened. When the groups reported back to the plenary session their recommendations were almost identical.
All were agreed that Canada must have uniform pollution levels and that these must be rigidly maintained. There was also unanimous agreement that the federal government should establish these standards, with the provinces being given the responsibility of administering them, providing Ottawa retains the authority to police the provinces.
January 21, 1970

Water Resources
This is one thing which is certainly not included in Bill C-144.
It was also agreed that educators have a bigger role to play in teaching Canadians the importance of a clean environment.
I am sure these conservationists feel that there is a place in the curriculum of our educational institutions for the teaching of the benefits of a clean environment and of the dangers of pollution. I continue:
Two of the groups looked into the future and decided that Canada will, some day, be short of water if she continues to ditch, drain and generally waste water at the present rate. They looked at the drainage authority in Manitoba where the municipality makes the decision to drain and it was agreed that authority should come from a less biased body. There was even discussion on the feasibility of underground storage for water.
It was decided that, if we can in fact foresee a time when Canada will be short of water, we should be making plans today and determine what can be done about it rather than waiting until there is an actual shortage. It was suggested, for instance, that if all marginal land were taken out of agricultural production today, much of it would return to marshland and this alone would provide extensive water storage.
It was suggested to me that the House should be made aware of the findings of this seminar. It is gratifying to know that groups such as wildlife associations are taking a keen interest in this very important problem. This group feels that in order for water in our lakes to be classed as clean, it must be fit for human consumption.
Recently a task force has been travelling throughout northern Manitoba visiting most, if not all, of the isolated areas. It has reported that there is more and more evidence of pollution in the lakes in these extremely isolated areas. This has been of great concern to this task force. Much of this pollution comes from the settlements on the shores of many of these lakes, but there is evidence of pollutants such as DDT. It is not too long ago that evidence of DDT contamination was found in polar bear carcasses in the high Arctic.
There is no use in believing that pollution is only a matter of concern to the urban centres. It is spreading very rapidly. When I was going to school we were taught that water would generally purify itself in a distance five to seven miles by running over rapids, etc., but this is not the case with the pollutants we have today. I have already mentioned the situation in the Saskatchewan River where the actual source of pollution is several hundred miles upstream. It would appear that the old saying about water purifying itself does not hold up under present day conditions.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
The problem raised by the pollution of our environment is generally considered to be one of major concern to Canada, and indeed, to North America as a whole. Control of the pollution of our waters, air and soil was determined at the Niagara Conference to be one of the highest priorities of the Progressive Conservative party, as something urgently needed for the preservation of our quality of life. Federal involvement in the work of pollution control has been spotty and uncertain. The first positive steps were taken in the early sixties by a Progressive Conservative government when grants and loans were made to municipalities for the installation of sewage disposal facilities. This was authorized by legislation.
During the past few years there has been an increasing demand that the federal government should involve itself in pollution control as a national priority-that the federal government should take firm action to coordinate its efforts and end the jurisdictional maze in which half a dozen federal departments pass responsibility back and forth. We are urging that the government set up one agency with which provincial and international bodies can deal. As against these desirable objectives, the proposed legislation has a number of shortcomings in its general approach. One of these shortcomings is that it deals with water alone. It does not touch on soil or air pollution. Even to the extent that it concerns water, it does nothing to improve interdepartmental communications or to sort out the jurisdictional fields among the departments.
At present the departments of Energy, Mines and Resources, Fisheries, Agriculture, External Affairs and Transport all have some kind of jurisdiction, as does the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. Nor does the bill make provision to establish national standards for water quality, purification equipment or monitoring. It is, in fact, still left open for one province, or one area of the country, to encourage industry to develop there by setting lower standards of pollution control.
I was gratified to see that the Canadian Wildlife Federation took a strong stand on this very matter. In addition, the federation deplored the absence of provision for any federal financial assistance to make it possible to achieve the objects of Bill C-144. The measure makes no provision for federal contributions to assist the provinces or to assist

January 21, 1970
Water Resources
those who will administer the water quality areas which are to be set up, and enable them to carry out their responsibilities.
Many hon. members on this side of the House have drawn attention to the alternatives which are available to the government. We hope that when the minister speaks later today he will give us an assurance that some of the suggestions, at least, will be considered seriously and incorporated in the bill. I intend to repeat some of these suggestions because we believe strongly that the government should take cognizance of the alternatives which have been put forward.
One of the our proposals is that the government should set up a national department or agency to co-ordinate pollution control efforts in all departments and that it should deal with water quality as part of this over-all approach. The bill before us is not part of any integrated plan; it is just another of these bits and pieces.
The second proposition we put forward is that the government should deal with water quality as part of a national priority to control pollution, and commit the necessary funds from taxation. We feel, also, that the government should ensure provincial co-operation before bringing in legislaiton.
In connection with this latter point, I should like to refer again to what was contained in the Speech from the Throne. On this subject of water resources, it stated that the government had made known its views on this serious matter and had begun discussions with the provinces upon the completion of which it would introduce legislation to enable it, in co-operation with the provinces, to improve and preserve our water resources. I ask hon. members to note the words which refer to the completion of these discussions. My understanding is that a further conference has yet to take place with the provinces on this very matter, and that it will be held in February. This being the case, I find myself wondering why the government should have brought forth the wishy-washy legislation before us at this particular time, though it was clearly stated in the Speech from the Throne that legislation would be presented only after conferences with the provinces had been completed.
We in the Official Opposition further believe that the government should establish national minimum standards for water quality management and provide for the prevention of pollution on a national basis, not just for special areas. As for the water quality

management area system proposd in this bill, it is only one of several possible approaches. Since the government has selected this particular one we shall try to clear up its many shortcomings and attempt to make it work.
In conclusion, I want to make it very clear that we on this side of the House are particularly interested in this subject and that we sincerely hope the people of Canada will have an opportunity to look over the contents of Bill C-144 and send in their own ideas as to the improvements which we know they will find necessary. We trust, too, that they will support us in our efforts to persuade the government to make amendments to the bill which would allow it to do the imporant job which faces Canadians in controlling, or eliminating as far as possible, the menace of pollution.

speechtext:
A few
months ago, Mr. Speaker, a meeting was called by the Minister of Mines in Ontario to discuss the development of secondary industry in northern Ontario. At this meeting there was a large representation from the community, from labour, management, the professions and the provincial civil service. A few federal civil servants were there too, to take part in a discussion on the potential of the area and how it could be developed.
It was an interesting conference, but what surprised me were the views of one of those present who told us, during the discussion of development of secondary industry, that as far as he was concerned he did not want any such development in northern Ontario. It would mean, he said, that the air would be polluted, that the water would be polluted and that the earth would be polluted. He lived in northern Ontario because he liked clean air and clean water. If the price he had to pay for this was the sacrifice of the development of industry, or of the opening of new mines, he was ready to pay that price. Any factories that wished to do so could establish themselves in Toronto where their employees could live in the smog, but he himself had no desire to do so.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
This surprised me because I had never really thought of all the things which are lost as a nation develops. There is a price exacted for everything and the price may sometimes be higher than the value received. In Toronto people who look out at the lake see the recreational facilities and perhaps decide that the environmental loss they have suffered

may not be worth some of the development that has been achieved in the area. However, probably the purpose of this bill is not to cover matters of environmental control. It is concerned mainly with the matter of water pollution. From my reading of it, it would appear to be a good bill. The criticism that has been made is that it does not go far enough, does not establish federal standards and does not make provision for the federal government to do the things it perhaps should do. All these are good criticisms. However, the minister probably does not have an answer to these criticisms because a great deal of money is involved. To date, the public has not really decided whether the price is worth paying. Until the public makes up its mind, we will have the type of pollution control the government decides to establish.
I do not intend to be nasty to the government. The government now has legislation by which it can control many of the problems that exist. Our harbours could be controlled by the National Harbours Board legislation which is very extensive and autocratic. The same is true in respect of the Navigable Waters Pro'ection Act. This again is old legislation which was brought into effect without fanfare. It is my hope that discussions between the federal and provincial governments will progress to the point where the jurisdictional problems will be ironed out. If we are not willing to invest the money in something, then we really are not in a position to do anything about it.
It is interesting to note some objections which have been raised by people at the head of the lakes. There are reports that the United States Corps of Engineers is directly asking Canadian citizens to provide them with water information. These questions have been asked over a period of time. The provincial government has become concerned about this and has raised the matter with the RCMP. The provincial authorities demand that this type of inquiry by a United States agency be made through the Department of External Affairs of the federal government or at least through the provincial government.
The federal government has indicated that it has no information about the problem. I have a question in this regard which appears on the Order Paper. The RCMP has asked me for information to enable them to make inquiries about this matter. In northern Ontario, and I believe throughout the mid-Canada corridor a situation exists in which Canadians are becoming perturbed not only 21611-29J
Water Resources
about our water resource but also about the fact that the United States authorities are looking at our resource and are applying pressure in respect of it in the hope that we will sell it. At the head of the lakes, individuals are asked to measure the water, prepare weather reports and so on and then are paid $3.50 per week. This information is being provided to the United States army authorities by 40 or 50 Canadians. It seems strange that the RCMP is not in a position to obtain the information they desire. However, I would be prepared to reveal the source of my information and I am sure other members from northern Ontario could do likewise.
I do not think most Canadians believe this is the proper way for our resources to be administered. It is being done this way because the Canadian government is not really interested in obtaining information. The United States authorities want to know what they will have to pay and the Canadian authorities do not have the necessary information available. It seems to me that in the mid-Canada corridor we will be faced with the choice of selling our water as a resource or keeping it, managing it, conserving it and enticing industries to come to the water rather than allowing the water to be diverted to the industries. Most people believe water is for drinking, for washing and then for dumping into the lakes. They believe that eventually it will come back again and there will always be nice clean water. I understand that where industries are situated on, and are using, a body of water, that water is used to the extent that even if pollutants are not employed it no longer has any friction reducing properties. Therefore, the normal properties in water can be used up by industry and the only way they can be replenished is by bringing in new water.
The United States authorities look at our water and think of taking it to the United States where it can be utilized in their environment. So, I believe we must pay some attention to this, set up a standard in respect of our resource and maintain it. The federal government will have to do this job. The federal government has the jurisdictional authority. The jurisdictional division will come into play when the provinces decide ta have their own standards. However, we have a responsibility to catalogue and conserve this resource wherever possible. The area which I represent may be called the upper Ottawa River basin. Those of us in Ottawa are in a position to observe the lower Ottawa River

basin. These two basins together make a very formidable source of water in Canada and that water finally ends up in the Atlantic ocean. Many studies have been undertaken in an effort to increase the supply of water from the Arctic watershed. The dividing point between the Arctic watershed and the Atlantic watershed is in my area. The difficulties in diverting considerable amounts of water from one area to another are not insurmountable. Distribution, however, is a horse of another colour.
I do not think there is any great disagreement between the people of Ontario, the people of Quebec and the people in other parts of Canada who are concerned about this watershed about having the water diverted to the Great Lakes where it would become a useful commodity in the United States.
Before we leave the difficulties in respect of the great Lakes, I would point out that there is now an agency in the United States which is deeply involved in the establishment of a connection between Lake Michigan and the Mississippi watershed. If this were established, it would eliminate some of the problems south of Chicago where the water is contaminated and is of no industrial or other use. It has become dead water. The only solution here is to bring in larger quantities of water from the Great Lakes system, which water of course would have to come from the Arctic watershed. The Canadian people would be involved just as the United States is now.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
I am more interested in this piece of legislation as it will affect the Ottawa River, Lake Timiskaming and the Upper Ottawa Valley. This area should be studied by all members of Parliament. All one has to do is look out over Parliament Hill and one can see and smell the pollution of the Ottawa River. Presumably, in Ottawa we are drinking this water. We are in a very good position to decide whether this large water source is being contaminated.
This river will fall under federal jurisdiction. I note that in this bill there are sections which will allow for control and the establishment of a water authority on Lake Timiskaming and the Ottawa River chain. They would allow for the control of that body of water, for the control of pollution and the establishment of an agency for the orderly operation of the resources in the Ottawa River basin. Therefore, I am very interested in this measure.
When my father went to Northern Ontario he went by boat. He went there in 1898 on a steamer that left Mattawa and travelled to Lake Timiskaming, visiting the various ports on the Quebec and Ontario side. All the cattle, mail and everything that went to Northern Ontario went in that manner. From reports I have read, this was a beautiful waterway and a trip well worth taking. Many people went as sightseers to observe the benefits of this newly developing country and stayed to become residents of that area, remaining the rest of their lives.
Lake Timiskaming forms a boundary between the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec. It is obviously under federal control. In the early days, transportation on it was controlled by the federal government. The driving of logs was controlled by the federal government. In fact all the resources that passed through that area, and there were a great many in terms of lumbering and the fur trade, were under the direction of the federal government.
In recent years, because of the establishment of a dam and the new use of that water, this authority of the federal government has been dissipated in a number of directions. I have a letter which was written in reply to a question by a provincial member of parliament for the area. He asked what effect the establishment of a dam at Lower Notch would have on the waterway. The reply came from Ontario Hydro in the form of a letter to the Hon. George Kerr, Minister of Energy and Resources Management, Parliament Buildings, Toronto. It reads in part:
The water level of Lake Timiskaming is controlled by the federally-owned dam at the south end of the lake, which is operated according to the decisions of a regulating committee made up of representatives from Quebec Hydro, federal Department of Public Works and Ontario Hydro. The discharges required through this dam and the subsequent elevations of Lake Timiskaming are a direct result of the rate of inflow to the lake. The Montreal River on which Lower Notch is situated contributes only a small part of the total flow, and daily flows on the Montreal will not generally be altered by Lower Notch. No change in the operating arrangements for Timiskaming is contemplated.
I live on the shores of Lake Timiskaming and it is very interesting to note how well this committee can control the level of that lake. The level varies about eight or nine feet. You must realize that the lake level was raised by some 12 feet when this dam was installed. This is a low lying farm area and the water level in the newly flooded part has risen about twelve feet. The people who own land in that area previously farmed this land.

When the water level rises and falls eight or nine feet, there is considerable difficulty controlling the flow. If the water level in Lake Timiskaming rises abnormally in the spring, then the people who have cottages all the way along the Ottawa River are in difficulty. If the dam on Lake Timiskaming went out there would probably be four feet of water over most of the city of Montreal. The lake forms a fairly substantial source of water, and one which has to be controlled over a large distance.
One of the problems that is developing results from the use or misuse of the water by both Quebec Hydro and Ontario Hydro who have not thought of anybody except themselves. This means they maintain as high a water level as possible, and to hell with the tourist operators, the recreation facilities, the shoreline, the pulp and paper industry, the logging industry and other industries using this water. The hydro companies believe they have a divine right as a result of their public utility position.
The federal government has neglected to use any influence it might have. The federal government built the dam and has repaired it on a number of occasions, but it has not really made any effort to see that the fishing industry has not been hurt. It has not been particularly interested in facilitating logging operations on the lake or in seeing that one of the greatest forms of pollution in any area- soil pollution-is controlled. It has not really done anything about the sewage which flows directly into this water.
If we are really interested in controlling pollution it seems to me there are enough teeth in this measure, if they are used, to enable the federal government to immediately supply the controls necessary for the orderly management of any large water resource. Such control measures would probably start in rural areas where dams would have to be installed to stop the runoff which carries a great amount of silt into the Ottawa basin. This will cost many municipalities a great deal of money. They do not have the money and apparently the provincial government does not give a hoot. If the federal government says it is interested in orderly management, it must be prepared to make money available to the municipalities for the basic control of water levels and soil pollution, such as the kind taking place in almost all agricultural areas along this whole water chain from the head of the lake at Notre Dame du Nord to Montreal. Unless the federal government is
Water Resources prepared to make this kind of an expenditure on behalf of the municipality, it really does not matter what is done along the line. It does not matter whether the river is polluted with chemicals or anything else if the runoff of silt is permitted.
As you fly over the watercourse, you note that a great deal of it is a dull muddy colour. There are hundreds and hundreds of tourist operations, both private and commercial, along this watercourse. These people have not had the resources to provide proper sanitary control. The federal government will have to make enough money available to them through CMHC so that they may upgrade their facilities.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
Many of the municipalities down-river are still dumping raw sewage into this lake. The minister knows this. When he lived on the Ottawa River I imagine that area got so polluted that he decided to move to another water resource area in his new riding, but I think he will find the same applies there also.
If we are not willing to make money available to the municipalities to treat the waste going into our water resources, then we can laugh at this bill. What would be the point of laying charges against some small municipality for dumping raw sewage into a river when everyone knows that the municipality does not have the financial resources to build the necessary facilities?
In Northern Ontario we embarked on a unique method of handling municipal waste. We put it in lagoons, and every year the lagoons freeze over very hard. When spring comes in the ice is quite high and these ponds are full. The one in my home town is situated quite close to the river. Water runs down off the hill into the lagoon and flushes it into the river, so that instead of getting a little pollution every day we get a lot of pollution during the spring run-off, but apparently the Ontario Water Resources Branch decided that this was fine.
Since the beginning of commercial development in Northern Ontario logs have been driven on the Timiskaming lake. In some places the bark and other things which come off the logs have polluted the lake to a depth of five feet, but no regulation is being drafted to ensure that the logs are peeled before they are put in the water.
I am sure that the departmental officials who drafted this bill have no intention of enforcing it. What they and the government

Water Resources
want is to have this bill to deal with cases of obvious pollution, cases where they will be obliged to do something. To this government, obvious pollution means sufficient pollution to kill all the fish in a river or lake. When they are found floating belly up, then the government will get after somebody and make him pay a few bucks. But, Mr. Speaker, that will merely be a licence to pollute.
The people of Canada are now concerned about the uses of water. They see the abuses perpetrated by hydro, and in some cases by provincial departments of lands and forests. In some areas these provincial departments placed poison in lakes to kill all the fish, but when they tried to restock those lakes at a later date they found it impossible to do so.
People are also giving considerable attention to the recreational and transportation uses of water. In the interval between two elections a few years ago, the Liberal party in Northern Ontario came out with a grand scheme to cope with the problem of Lake Timiskaming and the Ottawa River. Not only did they propose to bring barges up to Ottawa on the river, but also to bring them up through Lake Timiskaming. They were even going to take them into the French River and over into Sault Ste. Marie. But the Liberal party was not interested in controlling the environment of that water facility.
This is a nice bill. I hope all hon. members will support it, but it will not do any good. It is a sop to those people who believe that pollution has become a problem. In my opinion the government has no intention of providing enough money to municipalities or to provinces to establish the necessary controls. The federal government will not even make a survey of our water resources so that their orderly development may be planned. The only time the federal government will make use of this bill is when nothing else works, or in the case of a calamity.
For years the International Joint Commission has been looking at the problem in Lake Erie, smelling it, measuring it and tasting it. Every year the problem gets worse. We will never solve it until we decide to devote enough money to its solution. The amount of money that will be provided through this bill will be very small.
For these reasons, I say the bill is a nice one, but it does not meet the aspirations of almost all Canadians who want to avoid the water pollution problems that are besetting the United States. Canadians wish to develop the controls that will make it possible for

them to pass their natural water resources on to their children and their children's children in as pure a state as possible.

speechtext:
er Robarts, the Ontario government tried repeatedly to get federal assistance and cooperation in cleaning up the Ottawa River. When the Ontario authorities tackled this problem they quickly found that it was hopeless without the full co-operation of both the Province of Quebec and the federal government-the government whose job it is to take care of inter jurisdictional waters such as the Ottawa River interprovincial boundary.
It was no dice. There was no action. There was no interest. It was the same story when Ontario tried to co-operate with some seven states of the United States across the Great Lakes. Intentionally or not, the minister inferred in his pre-introduction publicity campaign that federal action was now being taken because the provinces had shirked the job. It is time to set the record straight. The failures of omission were federal, not provincial.
Finally, the federal giant has awakened. Unfortunately, this bill represents only the giant's yawn before rolling over and going back to sleep. The general concept of strict control of our natural environment-water, air and soil-we, as a party, support wholeheartedly. What we are attacking in this bill is the half-hearted approach to the problem. The utter inadequacy of the means so far advanced is illustrated by this shoddy piece of legislation. What we want to see is strong federal leadership, federal initiative to establish national standards, national goals, a national crusade.
In Canada today we have a very sorry and confused picture of antipollution effort. Some provinces and municipalities have done much. Many private industries have also done a great deal. Many private citizens have made an outstanding contribution. But the sad fact is that the federal government has done little or nothing and many industries and individuals will never do anything until the machinery to compel them to conform to standards of environmental control are established on a nation-wide basis. One cannot blame them too much. Until pollution of our air, water and soil is made an offence in every part of the country and until Canada as a whole proceeds positively against the threat, the industries and the citizens of the country are unlikely to observe antipollution measures.
To confine concern to a restricted list of specified bodies of water, as this bill does, is a useless gesture. It begs the question. It makes no sense to say, as this bill in effect, does say, "pollution is only officially pollution in this
Water Resources
lake or that river because we have been able to set up a joint board to control its waters".
What about the lake next door or the water in the river farther downstream? Despite the fatuous statements made the other evening by the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. Gibson) about water being different in different areas, it is obvious that water is water wherever it is when you are dealing with pollution of it.
We must have national standards of water quality. We must have national definitions of pollution and the offence of pollution. We must have uniform methods of controlling water and protecting it. We must ensure that pollution can be controlled wherever there is water, not simply in a scattering of designated areas under some cumbersome type of joint control board. Reading this bill, the impression is given that pollution only exists where there is a joint interest. What about all the vast areas of this country where the federal jurisdiction is paramount and absolute? I am thinking of the Arctic, for instance or the territories or the off-shore waters? Perhaps the federal government is hoping to set up a joint control board with the United States in these areas. Having heard the views of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources on the benefits of pooling continental resources, I can imagine that this may well be in his mind.
The truth of the matter is, Mr. Speaker, that the federal government has consistently refused to recognize the menace of pollution and has evaded its responsibility for leading a national effort on what is, clearly, a national problem. Now, it has suddenly awakened to the realization that Canadians want action and has rushed into the field too late and with too little.
Pollution does not stop at provincial boundaries. It is not susceptible to being neatly allotted to various political jurisdictions. It is all-pervasive and truly a universal threat. Pollution is a national threat and an international threat. The federal responsibility to act in this area is just as clear and urgent as it would be in the field of national defence were Canada to be threatened by hostile forces from outside our borders.
I find it amazing that the federal government is being so coy about invading provincial jurisdiction in this field and so scrupulous about staying within its own narrow constitutional areas. It never was so nice about things in the past. We can all recall the thinly disguised invasion of provincial rights and juris-

Water Resources
diction that accompanied the imposition of a nation-wide pension and medicare plan. Those plans were successfully forced upon many of the provinces by coercion. If such coercion were necessary and acceptable in the case of pensions and medicare, why not try a little in the far more pressing and serious problem of preserving our national physical environment?
The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) rightly pointed up the failure of the bill to provide municipalities with the sinews of war, the municipalities that are the front line in the battle with water pollution. This, I might point out, Mr. Speaker, is the very area in which, for the past 15 years, the Ontario government has been waging its principal fight by enabling municipalities to get capital at nominal cost to enable them to build and operate the sewage disposal plants and filtration plants that are the essential units of antipollution effort. I suggest to the minister that, if and when he ever gets around to trying to set up his joint control boards, he will find provincial and municipal authorities are already enjoying a wealth of experience and success in this field. He may even be forced to admit eventually that he and his army of experts have no exclusive jurisdiction when it comes to knowledge, ability and know-how.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
This, of course, is one of the great weaknesses of a generally weak bill. Nowhere in it is the fundamental question of the financing of water control measures dealt with. Yet this is vital to effective action. The absence of this basic provision from the bill is sufficient reason in itself to withdraw it and have it completely redrafted.
The hon. member for Bumaby-Seymour (Mr. Perrault), who enjoys the odd distinction of being unknown to his own leader, talked glibly of the necessity of getting the co-operation of municipalities and provinces in putting the provisions of this bill into action. He should know, and his government should know, that this co-operation can only be forthcoming if the federal authority is willing to get down to brass tacks and talk about the financing of antipollution measures. This question will not just go away if it is not talked about. There is hardly a municipality or a province in Canada that is not away ahead of the federal government in appreciation of the menace of pollution and the need to fight it everywhere and all the time. But

they know that effective action requires more than fine words and ringing slogans at a ministerial press conference, and more than a bill with more holes in it than a round of Swiss cheese.
They know that effective antipollution work takes money, tax money in massive amounts. They know, too, that they do not have that kind of money and little prospect of raising it from the share of the tax base at their disposal. I am afraid the minister and his colleagues are going to have to put their money where their mouth is if they expect to get the required co-operation from those who are already veterans of the fight against pollution.
The member for Bumaby-Seymour said at least one thing that made sense. He described this bill as "modest" and without any claim to being the instrument to "solve these problems". Perhaps we can persuade him to add his voice to the voices of those in this House who believe this bill to be completely inadequate and who believe it should now be withdrawn and redrafted.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is very difficult to evaluate the hazards due to water, air and soil pollution. As regards health, the present situation may be compared to a time bomb. In fact, the effects of pollution have just begun to appear but they will be felt more strongly within the next few years.
The wind may bring us foul smells, but it happens also that our rivers leave traces of dirt.
We, in the Quebec region, more particularly those of us who live in the St. Lawrence valley, have already felt the effects of water pollution, especially at the socio-economic level.
In fact, during the summer of 1967, commercial fishermen who had been fishing in the St. Lawrence river for several years and successfully earning their living and that of their family, had to give up their trade. In spite of the fact that two and a half years have passed since, many are still unemployed and have to be satisfied with social welfare allowances.
Fishermen enjoy a reputation of long standing and they are recognized as good workers. Those from the area of Quebec city and Trois-Rivieres did not rely wholly on luck, because they were well equipped. They owned very modern material such as draw-
January 21, 1970

Water Resources
nets several hundred feet long and enormous traps which change name according to areas and which are often made of various materials.
A fisherman does not really fish. It might be said rather that he draws up thousands of pounds of fish and, if all goes well, he may even assess his catch in tons.
Up to the fall of 1966 this was the situation in the centre of Quebec, on the St. Lawrence, between Orleans island and Montreal. Only in the fall of 1966 and in the spring of 1966 did it become tragic.
People who could manage with a salary of $5,000 or $7,000 a year saw this income reduced to nothing. In fact, all fish species- pike, dore, bass, carp and eel have vanished. And this is not merely a form of speech since the fish had been poisoned and was washed up by the sea.
We know that matters relating to water pollution are studied by the federal government in conjunction with the provinces.
However, since fish is disappearing from the St. Lawrence river, we must realize that the federal government and the Quebec government have never moved beyond the study stage. Highly-paid technicians are still pursuing studies; they do not exert themselves too much and they manage to justify their work in the eyes of the population by publishing a press release once in a while.
In my opinion, the most ridiculous step was taken in 1967 by the federal Minister of Agriculture. In the summer of 1967, if my memory serves me well, the Canadian government sent a pamphlet to the farmers in which it urged them never to dispose of old DDT containers in streams. They were asked to use any other means, for instance, to burn them or to bury them in the ground. All means except that one were good. The recommendation served to distract the attention of the people from the real problem, since, while the farmers worried about drops of DDT, the Expo Corporation was dumping into the St. Lawrence river thousands of pounds of rothane, a violent poison, commonly called DDD.
With the blessing of the federal and provincial governments this poison was used widely during the whole time of the building of the Expo site.
In the spring of 1967, 2,700 gallons of this poison, or 27,000 pounds, were dumped near the Expo site. And this criminal act was repeated regularly twice in 1966 and only once in 1965.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
Today, Bill C-144 is before the House. To my mind, this bill could bring the government to take a stand. But why should the bill come to us so late, after the damage is done? Provincial governments are not assuming their responsibilities, and we know why: because of electoral funds.
For instance, when a lumber company wishes to obtain a timber concession from the government, all it has to do is give money to the electoral funds of political parties. To be allowed to dump plant wastes freely into our rivers, big industries maintain a conspiracy within provincial governments through contributions to the electoral funds.
In Quebec, companies must supply the provincial government with a water sample. It is strange, however, that the sampling should be entrusted to the companies' own technicians.
Now, the technician is smart enough to know where to get his samples so as not to cause his employer any trouble. No technician would take his sample at the mouth of the sewage system of the company that employs him.
It is clear that "troubled" water would cause "troubles". I dare say his position would be jeopardized. Provincial governments were in no rush to note the danger of pollution because, as I said, electoral funds blocked their eyes and their nose.
Some companies that are developing our natural resources were not more honest since while they were poisoning our lakes and rivers, by dumping their waste in them, they sent to the responsible department of the province of Quebec a sample of pure water that was taken at the source of the streams.
One paragraph of the bill says, and I quote:
(g) "inter-jurisdictional waters" means any waters, whether international, boundary or otherwise, that, whether wholly situated in a province or not, significantly affect waters outside such province;
Since the water dividing line has not been established yet, I am somewhat disturbed. Unfortunately that has encouraged laziness until now, for many aspects of this problem have not been clarified yet, as concerns the St. Lawrence, for instance.
In a certain area, a number of people were using that river as a dump, throwing old automobile bodies into it. Below Trois-Rivieres, that practice went on until one municipality had the opportunity to lay a charge. So I sent a report to the provincial authorities who answered me that the matter

Water Resources
did not come under their jurisdiction, since navigable waters fall within the competence of the federal government. I was therefore advised to apply to the federal Department of Transport.
So I wrote to Ottawa and got the reply that the matter did not come under the jurisdiction of the federal government, since it had to do with trash dumped along the shores or into shallow water. The only thing that matters to the federal government is that the channel be open to shipping. It is not concerned about waste.
Confronted with a man sentenced to death, Pontius Pilate washed his hands. Today, when it comes to dealing with the Canadian waters which are a source of life, some people find it possible once more to wash their hands of the whole thing.
The federal government knowing that Expo 67 was under preparation, during the years 1965-1966, confined itself, at the time, to conducting studies on the waters of the Great Lakes. Let me quote a question I directed then to the government, as it appears on page 7462 of Hansard for April 14, 1969. Here it is:
1.	Did the Department of National Health and Welfare take water samples from the St. Lawrence River in the summers of 1967 and 1968?
2.	If so, did the analysis of this water reveal that there was a danger for bathers in (a) Tadous-sac (b) Quebec City (c) Trois-Rivieres (d) Montreal?
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) gave this answer, and I quote:
1.	The Department of National Health and Welfare has carried out water quality studies on the international section of the St. Lawrence River (from Kingston, Ontario, to Cornwall, Ontario), each summer since 1965. These studies were conducted under the aegis of a current reference to the International Joint Commission on Lake Erie, Lake Ontario and the International Section of the St. Lawrence River.
2.	As the studies have been limited to the international section of the St. Lawrence River, water quality data collected cannot be interpreted with regard to conditions in the vicinity of (a) Tadous-sac (b) Quebec City (c) Trois Rivieres (d) Montreal.
Mr. Speaker, barely a few days before I asked that question, I wrote to Mr. Lessard, the Quebec Health Minister, as follows:
Dear Sir,
A Quebecer would be interested in the rental of a public beach is now considering the possibility of carrying out his wish at one of the two following locations on the shores of the St. Lawrence: Cap-Rouge or Anse-au-Foulon, Sillery.
[Mr. Godin.)
And I went on asking-
-for a copy of the water analysis at those locations during the summers of 1966, 1967, 1968.
On March 4, 1969, I received the following reply:
Dear Sir,
I acknowledge receipt of your letter dated February 25 last and I wish to advise you that last year, swimming was prohibited at the Anse-au-Foulon beach by the Department of Health due to water pollution.
As for Cap-Rouge, we should have to know exactly the spot where the quality of the water is of interest to you.
Mr. Speaker, I remember quite well that during the summer of 1969, the beach at Sillery was closed to the citizens of Quebec City. On the other hand, I also remember that at Cap-Rouge, a few miles from there, Mr. Roger Lemelin, a well-known author, could still swim, as could the hon. members for Louis-Hebert and Langelier (Messrs. Cantin and Marchand).
Mr. Speaker, we must see the situation in its true light. The water from the St. Lawrence, dangerous to swim in, is the drinking water of the people of Levis. In fact, Levis, Lauzon, Bienville, Saint-Romuald, Saint-David get their drinking water from the St. Lawrence River. While swimming is forbidden on the north shore of the river, it provides drinking water on the south shore.
I hope that Bill C-144 will clear up the problem. Of course, those are extreme cases and I believe that the residents of that region are entitled to know exactly what the situation is.
In my opinion, given the facts, Bill C-144 could be a good measure. Will it be properly enforced, or used solely for political purposes and to foster small quarrels with the provinces?
We are aware that in our industrialized world, waste of all kind is increasing, both at the manufacturing and at the processing levels, and that to achieve high quality products, we have to get rid of a considerable amount of indispensable material. And up until now, waterways were considered as ideal dumps. The dangers of such a practice are obvious, and some companies have recognized them.
I want to mention the efforts of some industries to curb pollution, and I am hoping for an increase in the number of those that will co-operate to keep up the fight essential to our survival. But as always one has to think of the cost. Co-operation from industries
January 21, 1970

is necessary, but are all industries in good enough financial position to consider a water treatment program? Are all the municipalities which are considering an exchange program in a suitable financial position to fight pollution with means essential to the improvement of the present situation? This is open to question if we refer to a statement by Mr. Paul O. Trepanier, former mayor of Granby, who said that 75 per cent of Quebec municipalities were faced with bankruptcy.
Here is what I read on page 13 of this bill:
Water quality management agencies.
The objects of each water quality management agency shall be to plan, initiate and carry out programs to restore, preserve and enhance the water quality level in the water quality management area for which the agency is incorporated or named.

The other main thought I want to pass on to the House before we conclude the debate is this: I believe this question of the pollution of our waters and of our environment generally is part of a larger one having to do with the role of science and technology in our society. The day has come, indeed, it is long past, when we ought to have a minister and a department of science and technology in the government of Canada. After all, it is science and technology which are virtually making possible the kind of life we live today. We are aware of the things which have improved our lives. On the other hand, because of the impact of science and technology in the profit-making system under which we live, an awful lot has been done to despoil our lives. It is commonplace to refer to Canada as one of the young countries of the world. In fact it is one of the oldest. Few others still look, as Canada does in about three quarters of its area, just as they did two hundred and perhaps ten thousand years ago.

Then, Blair Fraser talks about this great area of our country that is largely untouched, an area which most people have not seen. But it is there, and to him it is a symbol of the future and the hope of this country. These are his last two paragraphs:
Meanwhile "development" continues. Canada's standard of living, second highest in the world (by North American measurement), is in no danger of losing that proud position. The legislation contains no teeth. It does not contain things that are necessary if we are to reach a satisfactory conclusion to the problem,. I will admit that the minister has taken a very timid step in the right direction. One recalls that the Prime Minister (Mr. Water Resources
Trudeau), when speaking on the just society, stated that some effective solution must be found for the control of air and water pollution and that we must move faster and more imaginatively in this area. I do not see much indication of that in this bill. No one will disagree with this statement, but the government brings in a bill which covers water pollution only and does nothing about air, soil or noise pollution. I do not know whether reference has been made to this in this debate, but I believe all of us owe a deep debt of gratitude to Rachel Carson, who has since passed away, for awakening us to the damage being done and our future position if things continue in the present manner.
It is interesting to note that people in several cities of the United States are drinking water from taps after that water has gone through city sewers. Now we come to the question: do we really need this bill. As I have said, it is a step in the right direction, but I wonder whether this bill, if it is not any better enforced than the fisheries bill in respect of our Great Lakes system, will accomplish anything. It has been shown that our fish in the Great Lakes contain levels of DDT above permissible levels. I believe we must realize, in our war on pollution of the air, water or land, that we can never hope to return to the time when waters were pure and the air was clear.
It has been pointed out by other speakers that DDT, which has proven to be a boon to the farmers, contains a particular hydrocarbon which retains its identity and decomposes very slowly. Some authorities put the rate of deterioration at about 20 per cent over a period of 20 years. This means it remains in the soil, in the water and in the fish and becomes cumulative. What provisions or thoughts are there in respect of providing something that will do a similar job for the farmers in their effort to produce the food we need? Dr. Jones of the University of Toronto, I think last December, pointed out that there were chemicals now that would perform the same function as the phosphates and which do not have any deleterious effects.
