Mr. Speaker, like the two previous speakers I will attempt to be brief because I know the minister wants to make some remarks at the conclusion of this debate and before this bill finally goes to the committee. In the few minutes I have at my disposal I should like to comment on this rather flimsy document we have before us, and make a few basic points.
Since I am very pessimistic about pollution in general, I will probably be labelled as a crepe hanger by any of those jolly chamber of commerce types who happen to be in this House of Commons. I do not believe that legislators anywhere in North America are going to do anything effective to halt or reverse pollution until it is too late.
My second point arises from the first. The problem of even water pollution alone, leaving soil and air pollution out of it for the moment, is such a complex and gigantic problem that to do very much about combatting it in a positive way, virtually our whole value system and way of life will have to be reassembled and changed. Our way of life
January 21, 1970

might have to be so dramatically altered that politicians would find little public support for the rigid measures necessary to overcome the pollution problem. I think I know a little bit about what the minister and the government face in dealing with a bill that would be strong enough to overcome water pollution.
Finally, having read the bill thoroughly, I am convinced it confirms what I said regarding my first two points in so many ways I am alarmed. It alarms me when I think of the future of those children being born today, because of the kinds of things they will have to face by the time they are as old as I am.
Everybody is in on the pollution kick today. Pollution is another motherhood subject. It has become such a popular word that everybody wants to get in on the act. But I am afraid Bill C-144 has about as much resemblance to any solution to the problem of water pollution as a stage backdrop has to real trees in the forest. I think the bill before us today is but a political response to justify the government in face of the public outcry for clean water. Regretfully, what we have before us is largely a snow job or, with deference to the minister, probably a "Joe" job.
The minister must be a little bit embarrassed in coming here to the House to smuggle the Canada water act past us masquerading as anything more than a government statement of pious hopes brought in belatedly to quell the clamour. There is probably a great gnawing fear on the part of the people of ultimate human extinction that certainly has not been focused on in this bill. Like the member who spoke before me, I hope the committee will severely tighten up a number of the measures in this proposal. I think perhaps if we closed our eyes, this problem of public concern, the public rumbling might go away, but I do not think the problem would disappear.
Population and pollution experts tell us that we may have at the most one generation, or by the end of this century, to find alternatives to the disasters we will face if we do not control our population.
World population is growing geometrically rather than arithmetically. We now have more than 3 billion people on this planet and by the year 2000 we expect to have over 6 billion. After another generation we expect to have, by anyone's guess, perhaps 25 billion. Some people say this will mean a population density in the livable parts of the earth of
120,000	people per square mile, which is
Water Resources
about the population density of the slums of Hong Kong.
How do we handle this kind of density in the year 2025 when today, in a sparsely populated country such as Canada we have dead lakes, poisoned bays, fetid, stinking rivers so laden with solid effluent you almost have to equip the fish with football helmets in order that they may swim unbruised to their spawning grounds?
Pollution increases are usually a mathematical function of population increase and population density. The magnitude of this problem is so little understood by the world at large and the Canadian general public, yet so crucial to our survival, that if I were a newly married man today, because I love children, I doubt very much whether I would bring any into the world, knowing as I do what survival conflicts they are going to face by the time they are 30 years of age.
I said earlier that the population problems are so complex that to alter them fundamentally would mean a whole change in our value system. I should like the House to consider for a moment the interrelation of the following points, and I will not elaborate on them: population growth and pollution, which I dealt with earlier; increased chemical disposal and pollution; rise in expectations or standard of living and pollution; increased industrialization and pollution; increased world and domestic trade and pollution, and increased resource exploitation, mining, logging, hydro, thermonuclear plants and pollution.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
I do not think anyone in this House, least of all the minister, can minimize the complexities of the problems facing us. Our task is to develop the kind of legal machinery and the kind of public attitudes that can cope with the problems, and I personally do not believe this bill is designed to do so. I believe it is theoretically possible to reconcile all of these conflicts of which I spoke, earlier but I do not think we are going to do it in time. I despair that we won't do it in time. But I think I have said enough to indicate and briefly document the serious threat to our survival that our present human behavior contemplates.
The concern for pollution should have a much higher priority in the government's scheme of priorities. It should be assigned a priority ahead of such things as the constitution and inflation, because what is the point in solving the problems presented by inflation

January 21, 1970
Water Resources
and the constitution if by the year 2000 we are all going to choke on the air that we breathe, and drown in polluted waters? Life demands clean air and clean water for survival.
This brings me to something specific about Bill C-144. I am sure it has been touched on previously and therefore I will not elaborate upon it. It concerns the means of implementation of the provisions in the water quality and water resource clauses of the bill.
From time to time I speak to and communicate with municipal leaders in my riding. I represent parts of nine different municipalities. All or most of these municipalities dispose of their sewage directly into the Fraser River. I suppose they have the choice of contaminating the land or the river, and like most suburban areas they choose the easiest way, the out of sight way. These men have expressed the fear to me that even with the best will in the world, people living in urban areas cannot afford to finance the kind of treatment systems that will be necessary and effective to combat pollution.
My riding is on the edge of urban growth. We know the extent of urbanization in our country. If municipalities on the edge of urban growth, together with the major urban centres, cannot finance municipal treatment plants, and have no means to do so, all the legislation in the world is not going to assist them. Therefore, I think we should be looking for something more specific in terms of financial assistance in the Canada water bill.
What we have here in this bill is but a federal superstructure, an administrative superstructure, that is to be imposed upon what we have already, and God knows how many different agencies we now have to deal with pollution, even just water pollution.
The responsibilities for pollution control do not stop at the municipal level. The responsibilities for pollution control cannot be passed from the federal government to the provinces and then on to the municipalities. Nothing effective will be done unless we at the federal level are prepared to assist the municipalities to do the kind of things that they know now they must do.
I am confident hon. members on all sides of the House have taken advantage of this opportunity to take a swing at industrial polluters. I point out that municipalities, public bodies, are also polluting, but do not have the financial ability to avoid it. Now, we have before us a type of legislation which vaguely suggests that some kind of grants will be

made some time in the future. However, at present when municipalities which want to do something about the matter apply for money through CMHC for sewage treatment financing they are told there are no funds available. That gives an indication of the kind of priority assigned by the federal government to pollution control.
It is a serious thing. As the hon. member for York West (Mr. Givens) so emphatically points out, urban growth and limited financial resources mean that the cities cannot cope with the problem without outside help, a great deal of help, and we have not examined nearly enough ways in which to help them.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say that the provisions of clause 5(2) disturb me, because these clauses seem to say that if agreements for water quality fail to be reached between federal and provincial bodies then the federal government has a right to intervene. To me this indicates that there is no real confidence on the part of the federal government that the provinces can handle the problem by themselves. So, what the federal government gives itself here is an insurance clause.
Of course, the provinces cannot handle the problem by themselves. They have not been able to do so up until now, and there is no reason to expect that they will do so in the future. When this bill goes to committee I think we should look for some kind of financing formula similar to the Fraser Valley flood control formula, by which there would be a basic municipal, provincial and federal contribution for any treatment project approved. In short, Sir, I would like to see more of the preventive medicine type of thinking within the Canada water act. Let us not wait until we have to use the provisions of clause 5(2), by which time waters will have become so blatantly polluted that they are of national concern.
Why aren't we looking at these things in advance? Why are we not prepared to set up agencies to maintain water purity, rather than belatedly trying to reverse a process that may well nigh be irreversible? I am disturbed by the fact that in this bill water is emphasized solely as a resource. To me, thinking of water as a resource indicates that it is but something to be exploited. True, water is a resource but it is also an environment for life and this aspect should be reflected in this bill. Water is something crucial to our survival. It is necessary to life on this planet.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the reason I am pessimistic is that legislators do not tend to think
January 21. 1970

far ahead. Most of us think about as far ahead as the next election.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT INCLUDING RESEARCH AND PLANNING AND IMPLEMENTATION OF PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will heed the admonition of my hon. friend. Maybe we have all, including myself, spent too much time on this parenthetical reference of mine to the proceedings in the House. The words of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who dealt with the length of the debate, rather tempted me to move into this area but I shall move on with the concluding speech on second reading. May I say to the hon. members whose particular arguments I cannot meet in the short time allotted to me, that I undertake to discuss the points with them in committee if they are not reached this afternoon.
At the outset there are one or two things I should like to say in answer to several of the last speakers whilst the points are fresh in my mind. First of all, in reply to the hon. member for Victoria-Haliburton (Mr. Scott), who criticized the federal government for lack of action with regard to the Ottawa River and who indicated that he felt the governments of Ontario and Quebec were prepared to move when the federal government was not, I point out that the federal government offered, well over a year ago, to do a study of the Ottawa River at its own expense. This offer was not accepted by either province. I do not wish to rehash old problems because we want to move ahead in the future in a spirit of co-operation, but I do not

believe it would have been fair to leave the record with the incorrect reflection that this allegation would have left.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre made some criticism of science in general and, again, while this may be slightly off the subject of the particular bill, I think his criticism is one to be considered. He advocated a science department or a specific minister in charge of science. I would merely point out to him that while his reflections on the importance of science in the world into which we are moving are valid, I think his specific panacea for the cure of apparent difficulties of governmental structure in controlling the scientific and research endeavours of the future was considered by the OECD in a report specifically about Canadian Science.
This report advocated that there should not be a specific science department and probably this is because science itself is becoming so pervasive that it probably would be impossible to have science assumed by any one department or minister without having an allpowerful czar who would direct every governmental activity. Science comes into almost every facet of government and every department of government. It must be the challenge of those of us in this House who have some responsibility in this direction to see if we can find methods whereby we can co-ordinate the scientific activities of various departments.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Some of the structures that have been created recently such as the Science Council, the Science Secretariat and the Science Committee of Cabinet, are attempts to achieve the goal the hon. member referred to without creating new and monolithic structures and without placing ultimate and overly great power in one department or minister.
As I say, I have heard some very valid criticisms. When opening my speech, I said that we do not profess to have all the answers. But the officials of my department have studied this question at considerable length; they wanted to know how we ought to begin tackling the problem of water pollution. They have studied the application of the law in many parts of the world; have sought for precedents, and have, after a very considerable period of gestation I will admit-but it was a very necessary period of gestation- advised as to this bill which the government thinks is best for Canada at this time.
January 21, 1970

May I say that there is no perfect precedent. There is no country, I think, that has solved the question of pollution or water management. We have sought to learn from those who appeared to have had some success or acquired special knowledge, because we wished to learn from their example. I believe that this bill, with such help as we may obtain from members of the House when it goes to committee, will be the best possible bill and will be for the benefit of Canada.
In the first place may I point out that there has been possibly a fundamental misconception on the part of many hon. members with respect to the bill itself and what it purports to do. I point out that the bill is not an antipollution measure. That is not the purpose of the bill. This is not a single purpose bill designed to clear up pollution. We think that this bill goes farther than any other in the proper direction. This bill is for the purposes of totally managing and planning the use of our water resources in future. So far as the cleaning up of pollution where it exists-yes; that is one of the things this bill would purport to do. At least, it purports to create the instrument which will do that.
But this, surely, is not good enough. It is not sufficient for us to look forward at this time to a bill which merely says, "All we want to do is clean up the dirt where it exists." We are concerned with planning for the future use of waters in such a way that pollution will be minimized, yes; but we hope to manage these resources a good deal better than in the past so that undue pollution will not occur in future and, further, we are chiefly concerned that we achieve the optimum use of our water in the future. I think if we start with that understanding, with the understanding that this is not just a bill to clean up the harm that has been done in the past, we shall see that the purpose of the bill is to enable us to manage better this precious resource of water in the future.
I think the last speaker in the debate took umbrage because the bill refers to water as a resource. I make no apology for this. Surely, in the technological age we live in, if we are to achieve at least a minimal standard of living, let alone the best possible standard that I am sure we all want for those vast populations to which the hon. member referred, we must indeed use all the resources we have, or we will not be able to achieve that standard of well being. Water is one of the resources that we must use. Thence it follows that we must use this resource differently than we have been up to now, if it is to
Water Resources
be of continuing benefit for those who come after us and for the increasing populations that have been referred to.
I should now like, Mr. Speaker, to refer to the main objections that have been taken to the bill and, in the short time available to me, I will try to cover most of those objections to the best of my ability and in some detail, and then leave specific comments to the committee, if I may, along with any other general approaches to the bill that the committee may wish to take. First, I think many hon. members objected to the bill because of its failure to prescribe national water standards. At first sight this may appear to be a shortcoming of the bill. When I started studying the subject I looked rather hopefully for some rather simplistic type of device such as national water standards which people would have to live up to and observe, and then, hopefully, our troubles would be over.
Further study on my part with the help of officials convinced me that clearly this was not a good approach. Let me illustrate this as simply as I can this way. If you had national water standards in this highly industrialized age and in this highly industrialized country then, surely, you could not expect to achieve for all our waters that standard of pristine purity existing in some of our pure lakes that have as yet not been touched by industrial development. I say that because if we were to adopt that as our national standard we could not, and neither could any other country that adopted these standards, have bodies of water as pure as Lake Louise or as the lakes in the north.
Not only could we not have that general standard, but we would not wish to have it. Water must be used for many purposes in industry; and if you are to have one national standard you would have to take into cognizance the fact that in certain industrial areas waters must be used for industrial purposes and that, therefore, it cannot be as pure as it was in the days before we became industrialized. If we are prepared to say that under our national quality standards all our waters must be only as pure as those say of Hamilton Harbour, where quite properly certain economic activities relating to steel production and other industries take place, we must also say, surely, that waters as pure as those of Lake Louise may be polluted up to the level of Hamilton Harbour because that is what we are saying if we accept that national standard, and I do not think that is what any of us wants. We do not want to pollute down, so to

January 21, 1970
Water Resources
speak, to those levels where water is used for industrial purposes. On the other hand, if we say that under our national water standards all waters must attain the level of purity of Lake Louise then, clearly, we are proscribing the industrial use of many of our water basins. That would not be economically feasible, or possible, or wise. Waters used for industrial purposes could never be as pure as Lake Louise. At least, that is the conclusion that we came to, and we therefore said that this was not a good approach for Canada. We do not want to pollute down any of those areas that are still clean. We wished to avoid, wherever possible, having standards so high that they would make industrial activities which are very proper in certain areas impossible in the future. The bill does not attempt to do that, Mr. Speaker, and 1 think quite properly so. Instead it attempts to achieve the optimum standard. I stress that word, because that word is the key. The bill attempts to achieve the optimum standard in any large water basin.
What does this mean? In a water basin that is used for industrial purposes and the disposal of human waste, as many water basins are used, and where we may wish to preserve some aesthetic quality and where, also, part of the basin may be reserved for recreational uses, the optimum standard will be at that particular level of water purity which makes sense for that particular basin. In a basin where there is no industry and where good planning may indicate we should have a resort or recreational area in the foreseeable future, there will be a far different standard than the one applying to an industrial use of the water. In such a basin the optimum standard of water will be at a much higher level. In some water basins where the proper and best use of the water in the interest of the region, and of Canada in general, might be purely for industrial purposes or municipal waste, the optimum standard might be much lower. I do not see any specific areas where this would be the best thing. I think in all areas we can preserve some of the esthetic qualities and some of the recreational assets of our water.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
I wish to emphasize the point that in our view a national standard would very definitely not have been in the best interests of having the optimum standards of water in various parts of Canada. In this variegated country, it is very seldom there is a simplistic answer for everything, that the same answer

will do in all parts of Canada. In my view with water quality, as with many other things, we will have different standards in different water basins, but in each case there will be the optimum standard for the multiuse of water in that particular water basin.
The second general argument that was made, and hit hard was the question of financing. There seemed to be considerable ambivalence in my respectful view in this regard. Some hon. members indicated we should have a fund, a great big federal pot from which money could be used, to solve the problem of pollution in the various regions of Canada. At the same time and in the same speech some hon. members said, oh yes, but the polluters should pay.
I took the liberty of imposing on the very gracious lady, the hon. member for Vancou-ver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) and asked her a question. The hon. member seemed to feel there should be a much greater federal financial input. I asked her whether in her view the polluter should pay and should that be the premise of the bill. If I understood her answer correctly it was, yes, the polluter should pay. With respect, Mr. Speaker, I do not think we can have it both ways.
I think the premise of the bill is quite properly that the polluter should pay to rehabilitate the water, at least to put it back in the condition in which it was found and, in many cases, to improve it. I think that is the proper approach because it induces improvement. It is an incentive to use the water in such a way that it will not be polluted. If the user knows he must pay in order to rehabilitate, he will set up his systems of production in such a way that he will not pollute.
There is a real incentive to non-pollution. If there is to be a large fund and the public is to pay for the cleaning of polluted water, I suggest there is absolutely no incentive to the improvement of industrial practices in the future. I do not think we can have it both ways, Mr. Speaker, by having this paid from the public purse and at the same time having the polluter pay.
The philosophy of this act is that the polluter should pay. This is quite properly a cost of production in the same way as municipal and school taxes. Just as in the many areas of public contribution that the private user of resources must make in the form of a stipend paid to the public purse, so in future will the cost of rehabilitating water be a very proper cost of production.
January 21, 1970

The other two main complaints that were made by most speakers were in the area of phosphates and the proliferation of committees. Because my time is about to expire, I undertake to the House that I will deal with these matters to the best of my knowledge and in whatever length and depth the committee feels necessary, as well as with the respective criticisms of individual members, in Committee.
I again refer to the question of finances. May I say I appreciate the municipal problem. There was and will be again the Central Mortgage and Housing fund to help municipalities, but I do not think we should skate around this too glibly. In the past municipalities have accepted the fact that disposal of their waste as well as providing water, education and roads, was a proper municipal charge. I think all hon. members will agree with this. Municipalities have said it is a proper charge that the homeowner pay for the disposal of his waste. There may have to be a reconsideration of the ethic at the municipal level to see whether disposal of the waste alone is to be a proper charge on the municipal taxpayer. Is not the disposal of his waste in such a fashion that it does not contaminate the water for future or downstream
Water Resources
users, in the ethic of tomorrow, the proper responsibility at the municipal level? I know the municipal taxpayer may need help to finance the capital charges required. I suggest that the user at the municipal level, as well as the industrial level, is the proper place to put the responsibility for the maintenance of the quality of our waters and the improvement of that quality.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, I undertake to answer the two further major points, as well as the individual representations of hon. members, at the committee hearings.
